ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
If I join the midpoints of the sides of the large triangle in the picture, a small triangle is formed. If I join the midpoints of the sides of this small triangle, a tiny triangle is formed. How many of these tiny triangles can fit into the largest triangle at the same time?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure there is a large outer triangle. The midpoints of the three sides of the large triangle are connected, forming a smaller triangle located in the center. Inside this smaller triangle, the midpoints of each side are again connected, forming an even smaller, gray-shaded triangle. Reasoning: Connecting the midpoints of the three sides of a triangle will obtain a medial triangle similar to the original triangle, whose side length is 1/2 of the original, so the area is 1/4 of the original. After the first operation, the area of the small triangle is 1/4 of the large triangle. Doing the same operation on the small triangle the second time, the area of the tiny triangle is again 1/4 of the small triangle, so its area relative to the largest triangle is 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16. Therefore the largest triangle can simultaneously contain 16 such tiny triangles.

method.method_draft: Read the diagram as a large outer triangle, with a central triangle formed by joining the midpoints of the large triangle’s sides, and a shaded tiny triangle formed similarly inside that central triangle. From the text, note that the midpoint-joining operation is done twice. Use the midpoint/medial-triangle theorem: joining side midpoints creates a similar triangle with side length half of the original, so its area is one quarter of the original. Applying this twice makes the tiny triangle have area (1/4)·(1/4)=1/16 of the largest triangle. Therefore 16 tiny triangles fit into the largest triangle.
